198.text: PagedKVCache: the core innovation behind vLLM. Instead of pre-allocating max_seq_len per sequence, allocate small fixed-size blocks on demand. A block table maps logical positions to physical block IDs, exactly like OS page tables map virtual addresses to physical frames.

212.text: Free block list, like the OS free frame list. Blocks are allocated from here on demand and returned when sequences finish.

213.text: Reference count per physical block. A block shared by two sequences has refcount 2, and that is what makes copy-on-write possible: a block is only cloned before a write if someone else still points at it.

214.text: Block tables map (seq_id, layer) to a list of physical block ids. This is the page table. Every read and write goes through this indirection, which is what lets a sequence's KV cache live in blocks scattered anywhere in the pool.

242.text: Copy-on-write, and this is the branch that makes prefix sharing safe. If anyone else still points at this block, the write cannot happen in place, exactly the check fork() makes on a shared page.

243.text: Take a fresh physical block for the writer's private copy. This is the only allocation copy-on-write ever costs, and it is charged to the sequence that diverged.

535.text: Sharing is only half the mechanism; the other half is what happens when a sharer writes. This section makes copy-on-write actually fire, with refcounts printed before and after, instead of leaving the branch in append as untested code.

536.text: req_0's block table before the write: the shared physical block, same as everyone else's.

537.text: And its refcount before the write. This is the number that has to change if the mechanism works.

538.text: Count the free blocks first, so we can show how many the write consumed. The expected answer is exactly one, the writer's private copy, rather than one per sharer.

539.text: A token the shared prefix does not continue with. Divergence is the trigger; a sharer that never writes never pays.

540.text: One more token for req_0, landing in the same logical block it shares with three other sequences. That write cannot happen in place, so append clones first.

541.text: Read the block table back after the write. A different physical block id here is the proof that the clone happened.

542.text: The block table now points at a different physical block, and that difference is the proof the clone happened. The new id came off the free list, so it sits wherever the pool had a spare block, next door here only because this pool is fresh and blocks are popped from the end.

543.text: The original's refcount dropped by one. The sharers that did not write are unaffected and unaware.

544.text: And the clone has refcount 1: req_0 now owns it privately, so its next write in this block will not clone again.

545.text: One block allocated by the whole operation. Copy-on-write charges the divergence to the sequence that caused it, which is why a shared system prompt stays shared for every request that follows it verbatim.

546.text: req_1 and req_2 still point at the original block, unchanged. Print it rather than assume it.

547.text: Assert the clone actually happened. Without this, a refactor that broke the refcount check would leave the printed narrative intact and the mechanism silently dead.

548.text: And assert the refcount was decremented. These two lines are the difference between demonstrating copy-on-write and describing it.

549.text: The property that makes prefix sharing usable in production: the cost of divergence is paid once, by the diverging request, and not by the sharers.
